Order No.11 Dated : 14.06.2024
1.

This criminal revision petition is preferred against the order dated 06.08.2021 passed in S.T. Case No.364/2019 arising out of Kadma P.S. Case No.46/2018 whereby and whereunder the petition of discharge preferred by opposite party nos.2-7, was partly allowed by dropping the charge under Section 313 of the Indian Penal Code.
2. Petitioner is wife and as per the F.I.R., she was married to opposite party no.2 on 29.05.2015.
It is alleged that she was subjected to cruelty in reference to unlawful demand.

On 14.03.2018, her brother-in-law Dr. Sanjay Jauhary threatened that she will be eliminated, as a result she could not sleep throughout the night and reached to the police station in the morning at 11.30.
It is alleged that her husband and her in-laws conjointly harassed her, resulting in her miscarriage.

sentences.text: It is submitted by the learned counsel that after investigation, charge sheet in this case was submitted against the husband under Section 498A of Indian Penal Code.
Learned trial court took cognizance under Sections 498A and 313 of the IPC against all the accused persons who are opposite party nos.2-7 and the case was committed to the court of Sessions.
4. Discharge petition was filed in which the impugned order has been passed.

5. The main ground for preferring the instant criminal revision petition against the impugned order is that learned trial court has exceeded its jurisdiction by meticulously scrutinizing the evidence which is not supposed to be done while considering any discharge petition.

In the impugned order,
it has been observed that there was no medical evidence in support of termination of pregnancy.

However, from para 14 of the case diary, it will be evident that cervical length i.e. pregnancy of one month has been stated to be carried by the informant.
6.

It is submitted by the learned A.P.P. assisted by learned counsel on behalf of opposite party nos.2-7 that there is no medical evidence in support of the allegation that the informant was forced to undergo miscarriage.

It is true that there is evidence regarding the pregnancy of the victim/informant, but there is no other evidence to show that she suffered miscarriage and that too because of the medicine being forcibly given to the informant.
Furthermore, the said date on which it is alleged that the medicine was administered, is June, 2015 whereas FIR has lodged on 15th March, 2018.
There is no other evidence to show that she had complained about this to anyone.

7. Having considered the submissions advanced and the materials on record, I do not find any illegality or infirmity in the impugned order for the following reasons:-
Firstly, the provision of discharge as given in the Cr.P.C. finds its place depending upon the nature of trial under Section 227 Cr.P.C. in Sessions Trial case under Section 239 Cr.P.C. in trial of a warrant case by a Magistrate and in complaint case under 245 Cr.P.C.
It is to be noted that different expressions have been used by the legislature in all these three provisions and that is not without reason.

Section 227 Cr.P.C. uses the expression that is as follows:-
"If, upon consideration of the record of the case and the documents submitted therewith, and after hearing the submissions of the accused and the prosecution in this behalf, the Judge considers that there is not sufficient ground for proceeding against the accused, he shall discharge the accused and record his reasons for so doing."

Section 239 Cr.P.C. uses the expression that is as follows:-
If, upon considering the police report and the documents sent with it under section 173 and making such examination, if any, of the accused as the Magistrate thinks necessary and after giving the prosecution and the accused an opportunity of being Guria Soni @ Guria Jauhary vs The State Of Jharkhand on 14 June, 2024 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/50538810/
2 heard, the Magistrate considers the charge against the accused to be groundless, he shall discharge the accused, and record his reasons for so doing.

entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: Section 245 Cr.P.C.

uses the expression that is as follows:-
If, upon taking all the evidence referred to in section 244, the Magistrate considers,
for reasons to be recorded, that no case against the accused has been made out which,
if unrebutted, would warrant his conviction, the Magistrate shall discharge him.
From the plain reading of the above provisions, it will be apparent that in a case of serious nature when it is a Sessions trial case, for framing of charge, there should be sufficient ground.
It has been held by Hon'ble Supreme Court in Yogesh v. State of Maharashtra, (2008) 10 SCC 394 "16.

entities.text: Yogesh v. State of Maharashtra, (2008) 10 SCC 394 "
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: It is trite that the words "not sufficient ground for proceeding against the accused" appearing in the section postulate exercise of judicial mind on the part of the Judge to the facts of the case in order to determine whether a case for trial has been made out by the prosecution.
However, in assessing this fact, the Judge has the power to sift and weigh the material for the limited purpose of finding out whether or not a prima facie case against the accused has been made out.
The test to determine a prima facie case depends upon the facts of each case and in this regard it is neither feasible nor desirable to lay down a rule of universal application.

By and large, however, if two views are equally possible and the Judge is satisfied that the evidence produced before him gives rise to suspicion only as distinguished from grave suspicion, he will be fully within his right to discharge the accused.
At this stage, he is not to see as to whether the trial will end in conviction or not.

The broad test to be applied is whether the materials on record, if unrebutted,
make a conviction reasonably possible.

(See State of Bihar v. Ramesh Singh [(1977) 4 SCC 39 : 1977 SCC (Cri) 533] and Prafulla Kumar Samal [(1979) 3 SCC 4 : 1979 SCC (Cri) 609] .)"
8.

entities.text: State of Bihar v. Ramesh Singh [(1977) 4 SCC 39 : 1977 SCC (Cri) 533]
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: In the present case, I find force in the argument advanced on behalf of opposite parties that there is no allegation with respect to offence under Section 313 of IPC against opposite party nos.4-7.

The only reference in the FIR is against opposite party nos.2 and 3 that at the time of her pregnancy, she was administered medicine by them in the year 2015 whereas the present case has been filed in 2018.
There is no other evidence to show that she had complained about this to any quarter.
There is no medical evidence of termination of pregnancy.
I do not find any illegality in the impugned order.
Criminal Revision petition, accordingly stands rejected.

(Gautam Kumar Choudhary, J.) Anit Guria Soni @ Guria Jauhary vs The State Of Jharkhand on 14 June, 2024 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/50538810/
